In the [Seurat intro](01_seurat_intro.md) you annotated clusters by hand: you
looked at the expression of canonical markers, decided what each cluster was, and
typed in the names. That works,
but it is slow, it requires you to already know the markers, and it is hard to
defend when someone asks why cluster 4 is a CD8 T cell and not something else.

SingleR takes a different approach. Given a reference dataset of known cell
types, it correlates each of your cells against that reference and assigns the
best match. It annotates **cells**, not clusters, which means you can also use it
to check whether your clustering is carving the data at sensible joints.

> **About this tutorial.** This is our own version of a published tutorial,
> rewritten to run in the course container — see the credits at the bottom for
> the original. The original is worth reading too. It is what you will find when
> you search for this analysis, and comparing the two is good practice for
> something you will constantly do in your own work: taking a tutorial written
> for someone else's setup and making it run on yours.

## Before you start

We rendered this tutorial with:

```bash
interactive -a cusanovichlab -n 8 -t 02:00:00
```

`interactive` allocates memory per core — 4 GB each by default — so that is **32
GB** in total. Note there is no `--mem` flag: memory comes from the number of
cores you ask for. The default of 1 core and 4 GB is not enough: the dataset is
large before we subsample it.

The code alone takes about **3 minutes** to run, but we obviously expect you
to spend more time on it than that. Plan for at least 30 minutes. And always
ask for more time than you expect to need. A job that hits its limit is killed
part way through.

Also note that when R runs out of memory on the cluster, the scheduler kills it
with no error message. The session simply stops mid-command. If that ever
happens to you, here or anywhere else, memory is the first thing to check.

## Setup

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| cache: false
library(Seurat)
library(SingleR)
library(celldex)
library(scRNAseq)
library(pheatmap)
library(viridis)
library(ggplot2)

# CHANGE THIS to your NetID.
NETID <- "your_netid"


WORK <- file.path("/xdisk/darrenc/cmm_523", NETID, "singler")
dir.create(file.path(WORK, "output"), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)


WORK
```

## Get a reference

`celldex` provides several curated reference datasets, and choosing among them
matters more than any argument you will pass to `SingleR()`. The reference
defines the entire vocabulary of answers available: a cell type the reference
does not describe cannot be assigned, no matter how clearly it is present in
your data.

Our sample is PBMCs, so we use a reference built from blood. `MonacoImmuneData`
is RNA-seq of sorted immune populations from peripheral blood, which is as
close a match to this experiment as celldex offers.

The first call downloads and caches the reference, which takes a minute. The
cache location is set by the container, so it lands on `/xdisk` rather than in
your home directory.

```{r}
#| label: reference
ref <- celldex::MonacoImmuneData()
ref
```

Each reference has two label columns. `label.main` is coarse; `label.fine` is
granular. Which you want depends on the question.

```{r}
#| label: reference-labels
table(ref$label.main)
```

Every one of those is a blood population, which is the point. A broad atlas
like `HumanPrimaryCellAtlasData()` spans many tissues, and handing SingleR
hepatocytes and keratinocytes as options for a blood sample gives it
opportunities to be wrong in uninteresting ways — with one of those, you would
subset to the relevant lineages first. Here there is nothing to remove.

## Get some data to annotate

We will use a PBMC dataset from `scRNAseq` rather than the object from the last
tutorial, so this tutorial stands alone.

```{r}
#| label: test-data
sce <- scRNAseq::KotliarovPBMCData()
sce
```

That is around 58,000 cells. Before we subsample or annotate anything, it gets
the same quality control you applied to pbmc3k in the
[Seurat intro](01_seurat_intro.md) — QC comes first, every time, and the point
of doing it again here is that it should start feeling automatic.

```{r}
#| label: to-seurat
pbmc <- CreateSeuratObject(counts = counts(sce), project = "kotliarov")
pbmc[["percent.mt"]] <- PercentageFeatureSet(pbmc, pattern = "^MT-")

pbmc
```

```{r}
#| label: qc-plot
#| fig-width: 12
VlnPlot(pbmc, features = c("nFeature_RNA", "nCount_RNA", "percent.mt"),
        ncol = 3, pt.size = 0) + NoLegend()
```

Look at the distributions before you pick thresholds. Cells with very few
detected genes are usually empty or dying; cells with far more than the bulk of
the population are often two cells in one droplet; and a high mitochondrial
fraction indicates a cell that was damaged or lysing when it was captured.

Notice that the feature distribution is not one smooth hump. There is the main
population, and below it a separate smaller mode — the low-quality cells we
want to remove. Where exactly you cut between them is a judgment call, and the
conventional 200 lands partway into that lower mode rather than cleanly beneath
it. A somewhat higher threshold would be equally defensible here. This is the
reason to plot before filtering rather than copying numbers from a vignette.

```{r}
#| label: qc-filter
pbmc <- subset(
  pbmc,
  subset = nFeature_RNA > 200 & nFeature_RNA < 2500 & percent.mt < 10
)
pbmc
```

Those numbers are a starting point borrowed from the Seurat PBMC vignette, not
constants. They are reasonable for 10x PBMC data and wrong for plenty of other
experiments — a tissue with large, transcriptionally active cells will have
many legitimate cells above 2500 features, and cardiac or muscle tissue runs
high on mitochondrial content for real biological reasons. Read your own
distributions and justify your own cutoffs.

Now subsample, for runtime rather than for quality:

```{r}
#| label: subsample
set.seed(42)
pbmc <- pbmc[, sample(ncol(pbmc), 10000)]
pbmc <- NormalizeData(pbmc)
pbmc
```

How far down to subsample is a real trade-off. SingleR's per-cluster mode pools
the cells in each cluster before scoring, so the smaller the subsample, the
fewer cells stand behind each pooled profile and the noisier those scores get.
Ten thousand keeps runtime and memory reasonable while leaving enough cells in
the smaller clusters to say something about them.

Subsampling for a tutorial is fine. Subsampling for an analysis is a decision
you should make deliberately and report — rare populations are exactly the ones
a random subsample is most likely to lose.

SingleR expects log-normalized expression, which `NormalizeData()` above has
produced. SingleR does not care that the matrix started life as a
`SingleCellExperiment`.

## Run SingleR

```{r}
#| label: singler-main
norm_counts <- LayerData(pbmc, assay = "RNA", layer = "data")

pred.main <- SingleR(
  test = norm_counts,
  ref = ref,
  labels = ref$label.main
)

table(pred.main$pruned.labels, useNA = "ifany")
```

Note what we did *not* pass. SingleR chooses marker genes for each label before
scoring anything, and `de.method` controls how. The default, `"classic"`, ranks
genes by log fold change and is built for bulk references — which is what
Monaco is, RNA-seq of sorted populations with only a handful of samples per
label. The alternatives, `"wilcox"` and `"t"`, are for single-cell references,
where each label has hundreds or thousands of cells to run a test across.

The mismatch matters more than it sounds like it would. Several Monaco labels
rest on four sorted samples; ask for a Wilcoxon test on four observations and
you get unstable markers, and since those markers are what the correlation
scores are computed over, poor marker selection turns into confident wrong
labels downstream. Match the method to the reference.

`pruned.labels` is the important column. SingleR assigns every cell a label, but
then prunes assignments where the score is not meaningfully better than the
alternatives. Those become `NA`. A cell with `NA` is one SingleR is not confident
about, which is more useful than a confident wrong answer.

## Assess the assignments

The score heatmap shows, for each cell, how well it matched every label in the
reference. Good assignments look like a single bright band.

```{r}
#| label: score-heatmap
#| fig-height: 7
plotScoreHeatmap(pred.main)
```

The delta distribution is the gap between the best score and the median score
for each cell. Small deltas mean the cell matched everything about equally well,
which is a warning sign.

```{r}
#| label: delta-plot
#| fig-height: 7
plotDeltaDistribution(pred.main, ncol = 4, dots.on.top = FALSE)
```

## Fine-grained labels

```{r}
#| label: singler-fine
pred.fine <- SingleR(
  test = norm_counts,
  ref = ref,
  labels = ref$label.fine
)

head(sort(table(pred.fine$pruned.labels, useNA = "ifany"), decreasing = TRUE), 15)
```

Fine labels are more informative and less reliable. Distinguishing naive from
central memory CD4 T cells from transcriptome alone is genuinely hard, and the
pruning is correspondingly more aggressive. Use fine labels when you need the
resolution, and check the delta plot before you trust them.

## Comparing SingleR to your clusters

This is where SingleR earns its keep. If you have already clustered your data,
cross-tabulating clusters against SingleR labels tells you whether the clusters
correspond to recognizable cell types.

```{r}
#| label: crosstab
pbmc <- AddMetaData(pbmc, pred.main$pruned.labels, col.name = "SingleR_main")

# A quick standard clustering to compare against
pbmc <- FindVariableFeatures(pbmc, nfeatures = 2000)
pbmc <- ScaleData(pbmc)
pbmc <- RunPCA(pbmc, npcs = 20)
pbmc <- FindNeighbors(pbmc, dims = 1:20)
pbmc <- FindClusters(pbmc, resolution = 0.5)

tab <- table(cluster = pbmc$seurat_clusters, label = pbmc$SingleR_main)
tab
```

```{r}
#| label: crosstab-heatmap
#| fig-height: 7
pheatmap(log10(tab + 10), color = viridis::viridis(100))
```

Read this heatmap carefully, because it is diagnostic in both directions. A
cluster that maps cleanly onto one label is well behaved. A cluster spread
across several labels may be under-clustered. Several clusters mapping to the
same label may mean you over-clustered, or may mean there is real substructure
the reference cannot name.

The single most useful summary is the dominant label per cluster:

```{r}
#| label: dominant-label
apply(tab, 1, function(x) names(which.max(x)))
```

## Annotating clusters instead of cells

Taking the most common label in each cluster, as we just did, is a reasonable
summary but a crude one — it throws away how confident each call was. SingleR
can do the job properly. Pass `clusters=` and it pools the expression profiles
of all cells in a cluster before scoring, then returns one label per cluster.

```{r}
#| label: singler-cluster
pred.cluster <- SingleR(
  test     = norm_counts,
  ref      = ref,
  labels   = ref$label.main,
  clusters = pbmc$seurat_clusters
)

pred.cluster[, c("labels", "pruned.labels")]
```

Pooling first means each score is computed from hundreds or thousands of cells
rather than one, so the noise that makes individual assignments wobble largely
cancels out. The cost is that a cluster containing two cell types gets one
label and you lose the evidence that anything was mixed.

That trade-off is the real choice here. Per-cell labels are a diagnostic: the
disagreement *within* a cluster is information, and a cluster that comes back
speckled is telling you either that it is under-clustered or that the reference
cannot separate what is in it. Per-cluster labels are what you want once you
have settled on a clustering and need a name for each group.

Note the two columns printed above. `labels` is the call SingleR made for
every cluster. `pruned.labels` is the same thing with the calls SingleR did not
trust replaced by `NA`. Keep both — the difference between them is the
interesting part.

```{r}
#| label: map-cluster-labels
i <- match(pbmc$seurat_clusters, rownames(pred.cluster))

pbmc$SingleR_cluster        <- pred.cluster$labels[i]
pbmc$SingleR_cluster_pruned <- pred.cluster$pruned.labels[i]
```

## Labels on a UMAP

```{r}
#| label: umap-labels
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 10
pbmc <- RunUMAP(pbmc, dims = 1:20)

p1 <- DimPlot(pbmc, group.by = "seurat_clusters", label = TRUE) +
  NoLegend() + ggtitle("Seurat clusters")
p2 <- DimPlot(pbmc, group.by = "SingleR_main", label = TRUE, label.size = 3) +
  NoLegend() + ggtitle("SingleR, per cell")
p3 <- DimPlot(pbmc, group.by = "SingleR_cluster", label = TRUE, label.size = 3) +
  NoLegend() + ggtitle("SingleR, per cluster (all calls)")
p4 <- DimPlot(pbmc, group.by = "SingleR_cluster_pruned",
              label = TRUE, label.size = 3) +
  NoLegend() + ggtitle("SingleR, per cluster (pruned)")

(p1 + p2) / (p3 + p4)
```

Read these as a sequence. The per-cell panel shows where individual cells were
ambiguous — speckling means either the cluster holds more than one thing or the
reference cannot separate what is in it. The two per-cluster panels are the
same analysis shown twice: bottom left is every call SingleR made, bottom right
is those calls with the untrusted ones greyed out.

Grey is not a cell type and not an error. It is a cluster whose label SingleR
declined to stand behind, and the panel beside it shows what that label would
have been.

Seurat numbers clusters by size, so the highest numbers are the smallest
clusters, and in general it is those that give SingleR the most trouble. Had we
skipped the QC step above, more clusters would have come back unlabeled —
filtering removed much of the problem before annotation ever ran, which is the
argument for doing QC first in one picture.

When a cluster does come back grey, the usual explanations are: a cell type
your reference does not describe, collisions (two cells in one droplet), a
cluster that is really two cell types the clustering did not separate, cycling
cells whose proliferation signature swamps their identity, or low-quality cells
that QC should have caught. The annotation cannot distinguish these for you.
Markers can, and that is the work: plot canonical markers for whatever you
suspect and see whether the cluster supports it.

Counts are a cheap first look while you decide what to suspect — high for
collisions, low for dying cells — though they settle nothing on their own, and
a small cluster of resting lymphocytes will look RNA-poor for entirely
legitimate reasons.

```{r}
#| label: cluster-counts
#| fig-width: 10
VlnPlot(pbmc, features = "nCount_RNA", group.by = "seurat_clusters",
        pt.size = 0) + NoLegend()
```

One structural note on the pruning itself. SingleR flags assignments whose
margin over the alternatives looks like an outlier. Per cell, that test sees
thousands of values. Per cluster, it sees one value per cluster — a dozen or so
here — so it is a blunter instrument, and a borderline cluster could go either
way. Read the two per-cluster panels together rather than relying on the pruned
one alone.

## Checking the annotation against what you expect

An annotation that looks tidy is not the same as an annotation that is right.
The check worth building into your habits is to pick a population you know
should be in the sample and confirm it is there.

Dendritic cells are a good test for PBMCs: they are a normal constituent at
roughly one or two percent, and they are close enough to monocytes that a
reference built from the wrong tissue will quietly fold them in. Canonical
markers are `FCER1A`, `CD1C` and `CLEC9A` for conventional DCs and `LILRA4`
for plasmacytoid.

```{r}
#| label: dc-markers-present
dc_markers <- intersect(c("FCER1A", "CD1C", "CLEC9A", "LILRA4"), rownames(pbmc))
dc_markers
```

```{r}
#| label: dc-featureplot
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 10
FeaturePlot(pbmc, features = dc_markers, ncol = 2, order = TRUE)
```

Now compare where those markers sit against what SingleR called those cells,
keeping the pruned cells as their own group rather than letting them drop out
of the plot:

```{r}
#| label: dc-by-label
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 10
pbmc$annotation <- ifelse(is.na(pbmc$SingleR_main),
                          "unlabeled", pbmc$SingleR_main)

table(pbmc$annotation)

VlnPlot(pbmc, features = dc_markers, group.by = "annotation",
        ncol = 2, pt.size = 0)
```

That is what we want to see: the markers are elevated in the dendritic cell
group and essentially flat everywhere else, and the label accounts for about
two percent of cells — right where a PBMC sample should land. The annotation
survives the check.

Notice that `FCER1A` and `CD1C` (conventional DCs) and `LILRA4` (plasmacytoid
DCs) all come up in the same group. Monaco's `label.main` treats dendritic
cells as one category; `label.fine` separates the subtypes. Which you want
depends on whether that distinction matters for your question.

Had this gone the other way, the two failure modes look different and mean
different things. Markers lighting up inside the monocytes would mean the
reference could not separate the two and your DCs had been silently absorbed
under a confident wrong label. Markers lighting up in `unlabeled` would mean
SingleR saw that those cells matched nothing well and declined to name them —
less convenient, but honest, and much the better outcome of the two.

One more thing worth noticing, because it is the same check running in
reverse: a small number of cells came back as `Progenitors`. Haematopoietic
progenitors are not a normal constituent of peripheral blood, so a label
appearing where you did not expect one deserves the same scrutiny as a label
going missing. Given the size of that cluster and its unusually high counts,
collisions would be the first thing to rule out.

This is the habit worth taking from the tutorial. An automated annotation tells
you what the reference thought. Checking it against what you know should and
should not be in your sample is how you find out whether the reference was any
good.

## A caution about references

We chose a blood reference for a blood sample, which is why this worked. Get
that wrong and SingleR does not complain — a cell type the reference does not
contain still gets a label, the closest available match, assigned with no
outward sign that the right answer was never on the menu. Tumor cells
annotated against a healthy-tissue reference are the classic way to produce
nonsense that reads as authoritative.

Always check the delta distribution, always look at what fraction of cells got
pruned to `NA`, and treat a label as a hypothesis rather than a fact.

## Save your work

```{r}
#| label: save
saveRDS(pred.main, file = file.path(WORK, "output", "singler_main.rds"))
saveRDS(pred.fine, file = file.path(WORK, "output", "singler_fine.rds"))
```
